body:
How Palaeolithic people obtained food

Palaeolithic communities depended mainly on resources available in their natural surroundings. They are therefore described as hunter-gatherers.

Hunting and gathering were complementary activities. Hunting supplied animal food, while gathering provided fruits, roots, nuts, seeds and other edible plant materials. Fishing and collecting birds or eggs could also contribute to the diet.

The importance of each food source depended on local conditions. A community near a river could obtain resources different from those available to people living in a dry grassland or wooded region.

The ability to identify edible plants, follow animal movements and recognise seasonal changes was essential for survival.

Why hunter-gatherers moved from place to place

Many Palaeolithic groups moved between different resource areas rather than remaining permanently in one settlement.

There were several important reasons for this mobility.

  • Availability of food: remaining in one place for too long could reduce the supply of easily available wild plants and animals.
  • Movement of animals: grazing animals and other prey moved in search of food and water. Hunters could follow them.
  • Seasonal plant resources: fruits, nuts and other edible plant materials became available during different seasons.
  • Availability of water: some streams, ponds and lakes contained water only during part of the year. Communities might move when these sources dried up.

Movement could also help groups maintain contact with relatives and other communities.

Choosing a suitable place to live

Prehistoric communities often preferred locations where several basic resources were available together: water, food, shelter and suitable stone for tools.

Rock shelters and caves

Natural caves and rock shelters protected people from rain, heat and wind. Such shelters were available in the Vindhyan region and parts of the Deccan Plateau.

Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh is a major example of a landscape containing natural rock shelters used by prehistoric communities.

Open-air camps

Not all prehistoric settlements were caves. People also occupied open-air locations near rivers, lakes and other resource areas.

Some of these places may have been visited repeatedly when seasonal conditions were favourable.

Habitation sites and factory sites

Prehistoric sites are sometimes described according to the activities represented by their surviving remains.

  • Habitation site: a place where people lived or stayed, such as a cave, rock shelter or camp.
  • Factory site: a location where people made stone tools, often near a source of suitable stone.
  • Habitation-cum-factory site: a place where evidence indicates both occupation and tool-making activity.

Hunsgi in Karnataka provides examples of early Palaeolithic tool-making locations and probable habitation-cum-factory sites.

The term factory here refers to prehistoric tool production, not to a modern industrial building.

Uses of stone tools

Stone implements served a wide range of practical purposes:

  • Cutting meat and processing animal remains.
  • Scraping animal hides and tree bark.
  • Chopping wood for fuel, shelter or other implements.
  • Cutting fruits, roots and other plant materials.
  • Preparing wooden or bone implements.

Some stone tools could be attached to handles made from materials such as wood or bone. Other tools could be held directly.

Knowledge and use of fire

Fire could provide light, warmth and protection from some animals. It could also be used for roasting food.

Traces of ash have been found in the Kurnool caves of Andhra Pradesh. These remains have been interpreted as evidence suggesting that prehistoric people in the region were familiar with the use of fire.

This evidence should not be confused with a claim that Kurnool was necessarily the first place in India where humans used fire.

Cooperation and daily life

Living in groups could help prehistoric people obtain food, protect vulnerable members and share knowledge about the environment.

However, the exact division of activities between women, men and children cannot be established for every prehistoric community. It is not correct to assume that all hunting was performed by men or that all gathering was performed by women.

Different groups may have followed different practices.

Prelims focus

  • Hunter-gatherers depended mainly on wild plants and animals rather than cultivated crops.
  • Movement was influenced by food availability, animal movements, seasonal plants and water.
  • Bhimbetka is associated with natural rock shelters in Madhya Pradesh.
  • Hunsgi provides evidence of early stone-tool production and occupation.
  • A habitation-cum-factory site combines evidence of living and tool-making activities.
  • Ash remains in the Kurnool caves suggest familiarity with fire.
  • Trap: Seasonal movement does not mean that prehistoric communities never returned to the same location.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 1, What, Where, How and When?, pp. 1–3; Chapter 2, On the Trail of the Earliest People, pp. 11–19; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 4, Timeline and Sources of History, pp. 70–72; Archaeological Survey of India, Prehistoric Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka, site description, consulted 17 November 2026.]

title: Palaeolithic Hunter-Gatherers: Food, Shelter, Movement and Adaptation

body:
The environment at the beginning of the Mesolithic

Approximately 12,000 years ago, the world experienced an important shift towards warmer conditions as the last Ice Age ended.

In several regions, warmer conditions contributed to the expansion of grasslands. This favoured grazing animals such as deer, antelope, wild cattle, sheep and goats.

People who hunted these animals could follow their movements and become familiar with their feeding and breeding behaviour.

Fishing and the collection of naturally growing grains also became important in suitable environments.

These changes did not occur identically throughout India. Local rainfall, vegetation and water availability continued to produce differences in the ways communities lived.

What distinguishes the Mesolithic?

The most characteristic technological feature of the Mesolithic is the widespread use of very small stone implements called microliths.

Microlith

A microlith is a very small, deliberately shaped stone tool, often made from a blade or flake. Microliths could function individually or be fixed into handles and shafts to form more complex implements.

Microlithic tools were frequently made from fine-grained stones such as chert, chalcedony, jasper, agate and quartz.

Types of microliths

Microliths occur in several forms. A useful distinction is between geometric and non-geometric varieties.

Geometric microliths

These have recognisable geometric outlines.

  • Triangle: a small tool with a triangular outline.
  • Trapeze: a tool shaped approximately like a trapezium.
  • Lunate or crescent: a curved, crescent-shaped implement.

Non-geometric microliths

These include small blades, backed blades, points, scrapers and other forms that are not primarily distinguished by a regular geometric outline.

A backed blade has an edge deliberately blunted or modified, leaving another edge suitable for cutting or for use in a composite implement.

Composite tools

One of the important advantages of microlithic technology was the ability to combine small stone pieces with handles made from other materials.

Such implements are called composite tools because more than one component forms the working object.

Examples include:

  • Small stone points fixed to wooden arrow shafts.
  • Stone blades arranged along a wooden or bone handle to form a cutting implement.
  • Several sharp pieces fixed into a handle to form a saw-like edge.
  • Curved cutting implements suitable for gathering or cutting plant materials.

Using several small stone pieces allowed people to produce varied working edges without shaping every implement from one large stone.

However, the discovery of a microlithic sickle-like implement does not by itself prove that the community cultivated crops. Such tools could also be used to collect naturally growing grasses.

How Mesolithic communities obtained food

Hunting and gathering remained the principal means of subsistence in many Mesolithic communities.

Common activities included:

  • Hunting wild animals, including deer and antelope.
  • Catching fish and other aquatic animals where water resources were available.
  • Collecting edible fruits, roots, nuts and wild grains.
  • Using traps, snares and other hunting implements.
  • Processing plant and animal foods with cutting and grinding tools.

The transition towards herding and agriculture

As people observed the behaviour of animals and the seasonal growth of useful plants, some communities gradually developed ways of managing animals and plants.

Early evidence of domesticated animals occurs at certain Mesolithic sites or in later phases of their occupation. Other communities continued to depend heavily on hunting and gathering.

The transition from food collection to food production was therefore gradual and regionally varied.

Wild grain collection is not cultivation

Gathering seeds from naturally growing plants is a hunter-gatherer activity. Cultivation involves deliberately growing and tending plants for food. Evidence that people used grains does not automatically establish that they practised agriculture.

Did microliths first appear in the Mesolithic?

Small stone tools and early microlithic forms also occur in some late Palaeolithic contexts. Microliths continued to be used in later periods as well.

Therefore, microliths are especially characteristic of the Mesolithic, but are not absolutely restricted to it.

Prelims focus

  • The Mesolithic follows the Palaeolithic in the conventional Stone Age sequence.
  • Climatic warming and grassland development are associated with the Mesolithic transition.
  • Microliths are small stone tools commonly used in composite implements.
  • Triangles, trapezes and lunates are geometric microliths.
  • Hunting, gathering and fishing continued to be important Mesolithic activities.
  • Trap: Microliths do not automatically indicate agriculture, and their use was not limited exclusively to the Mesolithic.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 2, On the Trail of the Earliest People, pp. 16–19; Chapter 3, From Gathering to Growing Food, pp. 22–27; INFLIBNET, Pre and Protohistoric Cultures of India, Mesolithic Cultures of India, sections on technology, subsistence and cultural evolution, consulted 17 November 2026; INFLIBNET, Outlines of Indian History, Pre-historic Cultures in India, section 4, Mesolithic and Microlithic, consulted 17 November 2026.]

title: Mesolithic Culture: Environmental Change, Microliths and New Adaptations

body:
Changes in settlement patterns

Mesolithic communities occupied a wider variety of environments, including rock shelters, river valleys, lake margins, sand dunes and open plains.

Many communities continued to move between places according to the availability of resources. However, some locations were occupied for longer periods or repeatedly used by successive groups.

This created different kinds of settlement patterns, ranging from short-duration camps to more regularly occupied habitation areas.

Seasonal and repeated occupation

A seasonal settlement is a place occupied during particular times of the year, often because food or water is especially available then.

For example, a group might use an area near a water source during a favourable season and move elsewhere when water or wild food became scarce.

Repeated occupation means that people returned to a location over time. It does not necessarily mean that the site was permanently occupied throughout the year.

Some Mesolithic communities also occupied relatively stable camps or settlements for extended periods.

Major settlement environments

Rock shelters

Natural rock shelters provided protection from adverse weather. They were particularly useful in landscapes containing hills, forests, streams and accessible food resources.

Bhimbetka and Adamgarh in Madhya Pradesh are important examples of prehistoric rock-shelter environments.

Lake shores and river plains

Water bodies attracted animals and provided opportunities for fishing, collecting aquatic resources and obtaining drinking water.

Mesolithic communities occupied lake margins in the Ganga plain and riverine environments in other parts of India.

Sand dunes and open plains

In parts of Rajasthan and Gujarat, prehistoric communities occupied sand dunes and nearby open landscapes, especially where water and food resources could be obtained.

Such locations could support repeated or seasonal habitation.

Evidence of dwellings and occupation

Mesolithic settlements were not always confined to natural caves. At some sites, evidence indicates the construction of simple shelters and huts.

Chopani Mando in the Belan Valley of Uttar Pradesh has yielded evidence of circular or oval hut-like structures in Mesolithic occupation phases.

Other remains at Mesolithic sites include hearths, grinding stones, animal bones and discarded stone tools.

Grinding stones could be used to process plant foods, including wild grains. Their presence alone does not establish a farming economy.

Important Mesolithic sites in India

SiteStateImportant association
BhimbetkaMadhya PradeshRock shelters, microlithic remains and prehistoric paintings
AdamgarhMadhya PradeshRock shelters, Mesolithic occupation and animal remains
BagorRajasthanMesolithic settlement on the Kothari River; microliths and habitation evidence
TilwaraRajasthanMesolithic settlement in the Luni River region
Chopani MandoUttar PradeshBelan Valley; microliths and evidence of circular huts
Sarai Nahar RaiUttar PradeshLake-margin Mesolithic settlement and human burials
MahadahaUttar PradeshMesolithic human burials and animal remains
DamdamaUttar PradeshMesolithic habitation remains and human burials
BirbhanpurWest BengalDamodar River region; habitation and tool-making evidence

What human burials reveal

Human burials are an important feature of several Indian Mesolithic sites.

Sarai Nahar Rai, Mahadaha and Damdama in Uttar Pradesh have yielded Mesolithic burial evidence. Such discoveries establish that people sometimes intentionally buried their dead.

They also show that Mesolithic settlements were places of social life rather than merely temporary locations where stone tools were made.

However, burial practices were not necessarily identical in every community.

Hunting, gathering and early domestication

Animal bones and other remains indicate that many Mesolithic communities continued to obtain food from wild animals.

At some sites, evidence also indicates the presence of domesticated animals. Such evidence must be understood within the occupation phase in which it occurs.

A site occupied over several periods may contain remains of hunters, herders and later communities. It would be incorrect to assume that all these activities necessarily belonged to the earliest occupation.

Prelims focus

  • Bhimbetka and Adamgarh are important rock-shelter sites in Madhya Pradesh.
  • Bagor is located in Rajasthan on the Kothari River.
  • Tilwara is associated with the Luni River region of Rajasthan.
  • Chopani Mando in Uttar Pradesh provides evidence of circular hut-like structures.
  • Sarai Nahar Rai, Mahadaha and Damdama are associated with Mesolithic burials in Uttar Pradesh.
  • Birbhanpur is associated with the Damodar River region of West Bengal.
  • Trap: Repeated seasonal occupation is not necessarily the same as permanent village settlement.

[INFLIBNET, Pre and Protohistoric Cultures of India, Mesolithic Cultures of India, sections 2, 5, 7 and 8, and site discussions of Bagor, Birbhanpur, Chopani Mando, Sarai Nahar Rai, Mahadaha and Damdama, consulted 17 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 2, On the Trail of the Earliest People, pp. 14–19; Archaeological Survey of India, Prehistoric Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka, Mesolithic occupation and tools, consulted 17 November 2026.]
